Spinning: An extreme motor sports

By: Lara de Matos | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Once deemed the domain of criminals, gangsters and conmen, Spinning has wheeled its way into local popular culture.

Unique Selling Point:
Finally recognised as a national sport by Motorsport South Africa in 2014, daring women - and even children - are now taking up the wheel of this traditionally male-dominated, adrenaline pumping pastime.

Summary:
The cult of “gusheshe” (the BMWs traditionally used by competitors) has infiltrated all aspects of mainstream pop culture, featuring in movies, music videos and TV shows.
Car spinning has become an outlet for youngsters – including females - from troubled backgrounds to band together, as this uniquely South African daredevil sport shakes off the stigma of its lawless past and gives rise to a whole new generation of petrolheads.


Further information:
Dangerous, fun and proudly South African.

The alternative motorsport of Spinning has been drawing daring drivers, adrenaline junkies and curious spectators for over three decades.
Conceived in the townships during apartheid, this precarious pastime was once deemed the domain of criminals and gangsters - not least because the car favoured by competitors was the pre-1993 BMW 3 series (known as a Gusheshe), which was the getaway car of choice in many a heist.

Over time, car spinning has evolved into a celebrated South African cultural phenomenon, featuring in films and music videos.
It's also the fastest growing motorsport in the country, attracting a cross-section of society: rich, poor, black, white, coloured, Indian, young and old - everyone's getting in on this rubber-burning, tail-spinning frenzy!

Press Release:


Spinning
Once deemed the domain of criminals and gangsters, car spinning has wheeled its way into local popular culture. Since being recognised as a national sport
in 2014, daring women - and even children – are going behind the wheel of this traditionally male-dominated pastime. Carte Blanche asks: what’s behind this
adrenaline-pumping pursuit?

Script:


MAIN SEGMENT:

VO1: Her pink BMW slips and slides across the small tarmac pitch in a series of controlled stunts, before she flings herself out the window of the moving car, to the cheers of the crowd. This is the misunderstood world of spinning…

LINK: Once deemed the domain of gangsters, spinning has shifted into the mainstream. And it’s the younger generation of drivers who are helping to shape spinning’s new identity.

VO2: 20-year-old Stacey-Lee May, 22-year-old Tina Rossouw and 14-year-old Jean Pierre Kruger, are among the new band of petrolheads determined to see spinning shake off the stigma of its lawless past.

UPSOUND: STACEY-LEE MAY Like, 20 years ago people used to steal cars and come and spin it as a victory, but now we see it as a proudly South African sport because spinning is only in South Africa… and we are trying to grow it. And me being a female and Tina being a female, we are trying to show the world that it's not about gangsterism any more.

VO3: Dubbed the Queen of Smoke, Stacey-Lee May’s daredevil feats - juxtaposed against her petit physique - have earned her a strong following within the spinning community.

VO4: It’s a mad mix of skidding cars, high revs, impromptu song and dance and, on occasion, disorderly behaviour that generally went hand-in-hand with funeral celebrations for criminals.

VO5: The car favoured by the drivers then (due to its perceived association with wealthy white people) was the BMW 325. Otherwise known in township circles as a Gusheshe, it remains the car of choice for spinning.

UPSOUND: TINA ROSSOUW Spinning back then compared to now is completely different. Now it's a family thing, it has a positive effect on a lot of people’s lives and it keeps the youngsters away from drugs and off the streets.

VO6: Tina is also all about breaking barriers. A soilder in the South African Defence Force, where she’s studying diesel mechanics, Tina is far cry from your stereotypical girly-girl.

UPSOUND: TINA ROUSSOUW You would always find me in the garage, helping my father, working on his cars, (rather) than being in the kitchen, helping my mother cook. That's how I grew up, so, I enjoy it. I have a passion for cars.

UPSOUND: DEREK WATTS Tina, this is a Gusheshe, BMW 325, but I'm sure you've modified it even further?
TINA ROSSOUW: Yes, this is basically your original M20 engine of the E30. I didn't do much to the vehicle… I’m running dictator management system, which eliminates the airflow metre that the car originally comes with, so if you have a problem with your car, you can plug your laptop in and then everything will just come up - what you need to do, you can tune the car, or whatever…
TINA ROUSSOUW But as you grow more into the sport, power is the only thing that you want - more power - so I'm fine with this for now, but I think surely I will put a bigger engine in…

VO7: Engine modifications notwithstanding, the glaring lack of safety apparatus raises the old question, is spinning dangerous?

UPSOUND: MONDE HASHE Spinning has an element of danger in it - not as dangerous as any other motorsport... We spin in these cars - there's no high speeds, only high revs…

VO8: Himself a spinner, Monde Hashe has taken on the role of Spinning Commissioner for the MSA, in a bid to bridge the gap between government and the spinning community.

VO9: Helping to bolster their efforts is the fact spinning is now regarded as an actual sport.

LINK: With its origins deeply rooted in the streets of Soweto - where it’s said to have started in the early 80ties - it was only in 2014 that Motorsport South Africa officially recognised spinning as a sport.

UPSOUND: DEREK WATTS There were attempts to make spinning a recognised sport years ago, weren't there? Why did it take so long?
MONDE HASHE It took long, because with government and MSA being a body, they have lots of specifications, which they call rules and regulations, and what they want us to do with our cars. So we said no, we cannot afford a lot of these things...

UPSOUND: MONDE HASHE … we have so much politics, or many politics…

VO10: While government and the various bodies involved continue to battle it out, for youngsters like Stacey, Tina and Jean Pierre, spinning is about personal empowerment.

UPSOUND: DEREK WATTS Stacey, apparently one of the reasons you got into spinning is because you were bullied at school?
STACEY-LEE MAY Yes I was quite young in high school, I matriculated at the age of 16 turning 17, so I was always younger than the rest, so they used to bully me, call me names, put me in the dustbin... And I used to come home crying and then when I matriculated my dad was like enough of this, we need to change you, and when I started spinning I changed, because I don't let people walk all over me because I have a voice, I can tell you that what you're doing is wrong.

UPSOUND: DEREK WATTS But you're not leaving it to the spinning arena, you are determined to go ahead with law and finance qualifications?
STACEY-LEE MAY Yes I feel that you shouldn't be stuck in one job, and I mean one day when I'm older the spinning is going to ware out-I mean I can't be 60 years old still spinning a car - so I have to have my education because education is key…

V11: The subject of age itself is an equally contentious issue in spinning.

UPSOUND: DEREK WATTS Monde, I’m surprised to learn a youngster, 10-years-old, can get a license to spin?
MONDE I don't think that there is any sport that starts at 15... I'm still not happy with the age turn. If it can go down to 8, I will be extremely happy…

VO12: Now 14, Jean Pierre - better known to his fans as Panjaro - was among those who started spinning at the age of 10. He, along with older brother Austin, ranks among the top spinners currently in the sport.

UPSOUND: DEREK WATTS So Panjaro has challenged me to be a passenger and no safety belts -
PANJARO No safety belts…
DEREK WATTS No helmets-
PANJARO No helmets, no nothing - and no fear!
DEREK WATTS Don't know about that...

UPSOUND: DEREK WATTS (exclamatory remarks from Go Pro)

UPSOUND: DEREK WATTS Amazing hey... shoo! Yo! Yo, yo, yo, yo! Panjaro, that was a ride of a lifetime hey! Well done, you are a driver of note hey, but jeez, you scared the hell out of me! Can't believe how you control this thing hey… A legend at the age of 14.

VO13: But while the youngsters are certainly ruling the roost, spinning’s charm lies in its mass appeal.

UPSOUND: DEREK WATTS Is this a sport for everyone - is it multicultural?
VICTOR PARDAL: I can tell you I've been doing motorsports for many, many years and this is the only sport in South Africa that crosses all races, faces and different shoelaces...

VO14: Victor Pardal is the founder of Southside Crew and is something of a legend in spinning circles. It was Southside Crew that gave Stacey her start.

UPSOUND: DEREK WATTS So how can I get spinning?
VICTOR PARDAL: … So you're obviously going to get first gear in, get the revolutions up (revs)... You're a little bit lucky because this has got a nice V8. You're gong to put the first gear in, you're going to turn the steering wheel ever so slightly to get you going... get the revs up to about four and a half thousand RPM and you're gong to drop the clutch.
DEREK WATTS: Just avoid the walls?
VICTOR PARDAL: That’s all you've got to do...

UPSOUND: (DEREK SPINNING IN VIC’S CAR)/ SOUNDS OF REVS ETC/ THEM COMMENTING

VO15: So while spinning may be new to the likes of me, it’s touted as the fastest growing motorsport in the country. But, Stacey, for one, would like to see spinning go global.

UPSOUND:
DEREK WATTS Where do you want this sport to go?
STACEY-LEE MAY I would like to go and spin under the Eiffel tower in Paris one day - so I would like to see spinning all over the world, and I would also like to open a spinning school to teach young girls about mechanics and spinning-we should be able to have a wide variety, because you know they say females can't build engines, so I want to make that available for all females to know that, you can do anything.


PROMO 1:
VO: Once deemed the domain of gangsters, spinning has shifted into the mainstream. And it's the hunger generation of drivers who are helping to shape spinnings new identity.
UPSOUND: TINA ROSSOUW - I enjoy it. I have a passion for cars.

PROMO 2:
VO: It started in the townships, but now it's an official motorsport for young and old. Spinning is screeching its way into the limelight.
Cutaways of Stacey spinning and Derek in Panjaro's car.

TEASER:
LINK: (Derek on camera): It started in the townships, but now it's an official motorsport for young and old. Spinning is screeching its way into the limelight.
Cutaways of Stacey revving her car and pulling off.
